utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can you cite the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. We are Thursday, 15th of May, 2008. I would like to greet the members of the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj. First, a few housekeeping matters, but first I would like to ask for a closed session. I have a decision to communicate in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're in open session. I would like to inform Mr. Seselj that the internet connection is working, so normally the entire world can follow this hearing. Mr. Mundis, would you like to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, and to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, apparently this motion is confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps the Chamber ordered it to be filed eventually. It's certainly not indicated thus on the cover of the document. Perhaps for the benefit of the doubt, we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to private session, then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, I think the witness is waiting outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honours. There are two points I would like to address briefly. I would like to introduce the intern who is assisting us today, who -- her name is Sara Grujin. It's the first time she's with us today. Also a procedural matter I would like to address. The Court binder of the next witness is not quite as complete as it should be. We mentioned a video. I intend showing two video clips, one clip which has no sound and no transcript. The other one is very short. It's silent --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, interpreter's correction: I have handed out the transcript of the second video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not what the person is saying in the video clip that I'm interested in. It's just to be able to identify the person that I wish to show this video. These are two matters that I wished to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber because it was not mentioned in the Court binder which we prepared at the last minute given we had to replace a witness wasn't able to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you still confirm that you need two and a half hours for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I shall try and make it shorter, if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Whatever the case may be, we shall listen to all of this extremely carefully, and let's bring in the witness into the courtroom, please. In the meantime, Mr. Mundis, as far as next week is concerned, the upcoming witnesses, well, there's a fair chance that this witness today will have to come back on Tuesday. What happens after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The next scheduled witness, Professor Riedlmayer, would then testify immediately upon the conclusion of the current witness's testimony. Of course, in the event that the next witness is not able to remain, it might be the case -- I don't know, it might be the case that he has to return home and would need to return at a later date to complete his testimony. I simply don't know. I haven't spoken to the witness about that possibility. We would then immediately go to Dr. Riedlmayer on Tuesday. But the plan would be once this witness is complete, to immediately go to Dr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall put the question to him directly. Good afternoon, sir. I would like to check that our technical equipment is working properly. If you can hear me, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I'm able to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, can you give me your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Asim Alic. I was born on the 8th of March, 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, do you have a job currently, and if so, what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have an occupation currently or do you not do anything?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not catch it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, are you currently employed? Do you have an occupation or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, I am working. Yes, I do have a job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what do you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work for the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a police inspector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, have you ever before testified before a court of law on questions relating to the former Yugoslavia or is it the first time you testify today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I testified before the Special Court in Belgrade two years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you testified before the Special Court in Belgrade. Who did you testify against?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The case which was against Mr. Brano Grujic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, is this trial still ongoing or has there been a judgement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure. I believe that the case is still going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, please take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have something to share with you which is of a practical nature. Since we are running late, there was a witness who came to testify before you, and we can only hear you today. According to our schedule, you will have to resume your testimony next week, i.e., on Tuesday, which means that you would have to stay over until Tuesday. Is that a major problem for you or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you will spend the weekend here, and I hope the weather will remain fine. Sir, let me just inform you about the way in which these proceedings will unfold. Since you are a police inspector, you have some understanding and knowledge of what a court case is about. Today, this is a special court. The Judges are not the main protagonists, unfortunately, as far as I'm concerned, and this trial is conducted by the parties, which means that it is the Prosecutor who will put questions to you, first of all, and he will put questions to you and show documents to you. He will show you videos, since he told us that that was his intention. After that stage, Mr. Seselj, who's sitting on your left, will have the same time as the Prosecution to put questions to you, and that is part of what we call the cross-examination. I would like you to rest assured the cross-examination has two purposes; (a), test the credibility of the witness, so some questions will relate to your credibility, and, (b), the second part of the cross-examination is devoted to the substance of the case, based on the answers you gave the Prosecutor. The three Judges who form the Bench, who are in front of you, fortunately have rules of procedure which have entitled us to put questions also, and you will see that we will put questions to you. Generally, we put our questions once each party has put its questions, and our questions usually relate to the merits of the case. Please try and be as accurate as you can when you answer the questions, because all your answers will be recorded on the screen you have before you. It's in English, unfortunately for you, and you might not understand what's being said, but all of this is translated in realtime and is recorded in English on your screen. This is why it is most important that the questions are concise and that the answers are concise. If you don't understand the meaning of a question, please turn to the person who has put the question to you and ask this person to rephrase the question. As a rule, we have a break every hour and a half, and we have a 20-minute break, sometimes a 15-minute break. Today, we shall finish at 6.00 p.m., so we have three hours before us, and this is an exception. If at any point in time you do not feel well, do not hesitate to raise your hand so that we may adjourn the hearing, and I will adjourn instantly if you have such a problem. And the Bench will answer any questions you may have. I would also like to draw your attention to the fact that from now on you are a witness of the Court, which means that you cannot have any contacts with the Prosecution. You are going to stay here over the weekend, and you cannot contact the Prosecution. You are prohibited and banned from doing so. And the same applies to the Defence. So much for the information I wish to share with you. The Prosecutor, you have the floor, and the clock is beginning to tick. Thank you very much. It is 3.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Alic, when did you join the police, on what date?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I joined the police in October 1983, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You answered my second question, which was: In which town? Which unit in Belgrade did you join?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade, in the City Secretariat, I joined the Police Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Until when did you keep your position in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Until October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where were you posted?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: After that, I started working for the Public Security Station in Zvornik, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who was commander of the police forces in Zvornik when you got there in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Dragan Spasojevic. Mr. Dragan Spasojevic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Was there someone above him or was he the police officer with the highest rank?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: No, there was the chief of the Police Administration, who was hierarchically above him, and his name was Osman Mustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you briefly describe to us how the various departments in the Zvornik police were organised when you got there in 1991? Was there a traffic police department, a crime investigation department? Could you briefly tell us how the police was organised in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. The police was organised in this way: There was a chief of the Police Administration. He was the general chief of the police. Then there was the commander or the commander of the police station who had three assistants. One of the assistants was for the general police. A second assistant was for crime affairs. And the third assistant was for the regulation and control of traffic. In addition to that, there was also a section of the crime police as well as an administrative and support section.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll get back to these various departments, but before that: Do you remember how many active policemen were working in Zvornik when you got there in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: It was between 110 and 120 active policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: The complete force -- the complete police force was balanced. The ratio was approximately 50 per cent Bosniaks and 50 per cent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that there was a crime investigation department. Who headed that department?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fadil Mujic was the chief of the criminal police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who headed the general police force?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marinko Vasilic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who headed the traffic police department?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Mr. Slavko Eric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who headed the administrative unit of the police?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Madam Sehija Taljic was the chief of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And you, yourself, you were in charge of what unit, what department? What was your position in the police station?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I was one of the assistants of the commander of the police station. According to the decision assigning me to my work post at that moment in time. And at the same time, I also acted as deputy commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. And the commander of the police station was Barijovic [as interpreted]. I think that's the name you mentioned, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who is Marinko Vasilic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Marinko Vasilic was one of the assistant commanders of the commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I shall rephrase my question. What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: At some point, did you call on reserve policemen? I don't mean you, personally. I mean your police station.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. In October 1991. In October 1991, we were given an order by the then Republican Secretariat of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the effect that we were to mobilise a complete reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Overall, this reserve police force amounted to how many men?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Their number was double that of the active policemen on the active force, so it was between 110 and 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you specify? Are you saying that there were 220 reservists or are you saying there were reservists plus the active policemen amounted to double the amount of active policemen?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: The number of the reservists was equal to that of active policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's perfectly clear. After the call-up, did all these men remain in Zvornik or were they dispatched here and there and sent to various police stations?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: After mobilisation, these forces did not all remain in the town of Zvornik. They were assigned to another five localities in the Zvornik Municipalities; namely, five police stations or branch stations, substations, were established in five different locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Would you list us the names of these places, please?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: One of the police stations remained at the seat in the town of Zvornik, and it was in the same building as the Public Security Station of the town of Zvornik. Then there was another police station that was set up in the village of Orahovac. Another one was set up in a place called Sapna, and the third one in Kozluk, another one in Pilica, and another a fifth one in Drinjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. How many men were there, on average, per police station? And what I mean by that is I mean this includes the active policemen and the reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: That particular moment in time, we could not assign more than 10 to 15 active policemen to these branch stations or 15 to 20 reserve policemen, which in total was about 30 or 35 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: The Sapna, Orahovac and Kozluk, these police stations -- well, the commanders of these police stations reported to whom?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: They all reported to the police station commander in Zvornik and of course to the chief who was the overall commander, the overall chief of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you talk about the overall chief, commander of the police, could you give us his name again, please?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: The chief of the Public Security Station was Osman Mustafic, and the commander, commandeer, was Dragan Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember having been proofed Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of this week?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you remember having drawn a diagram of the police station at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to display Exhibit number 65 ter 7225, please. We have a translation that arrived rather late today. It's not in the binder, but it is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, do you recognise this document as being the diagram you drew of the police station in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you recognise your signature at the bottom of this document? There it is.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document into evidence, so please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could we have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P438.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, on this sketch, which -- we can see that Mustafic is Mr. Spasojevic's superior. Could you tell us in what circumstances Mustafic headed the SBS and that things didn't happen the other way around?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: After the elections in Zvornik Municipality and the victory by one of the parties, the party that was victorious, that won, they had the key posts in the municipality, and in all these organs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us more? Could you tell us which elections you are talking about? On what date did these take place?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I was working in Belgrade at the time, not in Zvornik, in the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us which party won the elections?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: In Zvornik Municipality, it was the SDA party that won, and it was at its proposal that the Osman Mustafic came to be the chief, and the SDS provided the second post.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you specify what SDS and SDA mean?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: The SDA is the Democratic Action Party, and the SDS is the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And SDA had a particular ethnicity? What part of the population did they represent?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: They were mostly parties that rallied exclusively a population from that same ethnic group. So the SDA rallied Muslims, Bosniaks, and the Serbian Democratic Party rallied Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the -- what were the ethnic groups in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Zvornik Municipality had a population of about 80.000. Of that number, 51 per cent were Muslims, 47 or 8 per cent were Serbs, and the rest were others; that is to say, Croats, Romanians and so on, all the other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the ethnic makeup of Mali Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Mali Zvornik is located in Serbia, but even there the population is mixed. I can't give you the percentages, but I do know that there were many Muslims living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to remain on the issue of political forces, can you tell us who the mayor of Zvornik was until April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: The mayor was Abdulah Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Is what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim, and he was from the SDA, the Democratic Action Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who is Alija Kapidzic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Alija Kapidzic was the chief of the National Defence Department, and he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Was he a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What other names of people belonging to the SDA in Zvornik can you remember at the time?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I can't remember any names now. I wouldn't want to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay. Who set up the SDS in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: The SDS of Zvornik was a municipal organisation of the Serbian Democratic Party, and Mr. Brano Grujic headed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who were the other leading members of the local branch of SDS in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I think there was Jovo Ivanovic, who was the President of Executive Power in Zvornik Municipality, and some other people whom I couldn't name now, because I don't want to get it wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Was Dragan Spasojevic a member of the SDS in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Dragan Spasojevic was appointed commander of the Public Security Station in Zvornik, as being a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know if he had relations with Brano Grujic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They would see each other often at the police station. I would see them there, and I attended their meetings regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What did Dragan Spasojevic call Brano Grujic; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: He called him "Big Daddy or "Veliki Tata." That's what he called him. For whatever reason, I can't say; that he liked him or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Which brings me back a little bit. When you're saying that Dragan Spasojevic headed the SDS in Zvornik, do you mean that he was the chairman? What was his title, exactly, within the SDS in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: The president of the SDS. That's how my perception of him was, the president of the Serbian Democratic Party, that was his political function.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know if Brano Grujic had relations with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you describe the relations between Brano Grujic and Arkan, and how do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I happen to know that because I was present on two occasions at Crisis Staff meetings that were held at the time, and Abdulah Pasic, the president of the municipality, held talks exclusively with the opposite side, if I can put it there, his opposite number, and that was the Serbian Democratic Party. Brano Grujic did maintain contacts with Arkan, because he called Arkan and his forces to come to Zvornik to help him out in taking over power and authority, taking over control there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you see Brano Grujic and Arkan together?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Then how do you know that Brano Grujic had contacts with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: That's what he -- what Abdulah Pasic told us. Upon returning from the meeting with Arkan, he reported to us and informed us what the topics of discussion were and how the discussion evolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? What did he tell you, exactly? Did he see both men together? What was his information based on, regarding relations between Arkan and Brano Grujic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I can explain it in the following way: When the meeting was organised in Mali Zvornik, at the Jezero Hotel, the meeting was organised with Arkan, and the mediator was Mr. Grujic. He was the go-between. And they all found -- they all happened to be at Jezero Hotel, Alija Kapidzic, Pasic and all the people there that were there at the time. They had discussions there. They discussed the problems that were looming, the ultimatum of the Serbian Democratic Party and Arkan, that the Bosniaks in the town of Zvornik should lay down their arms, hand over power and authority. And when Abdulah Pasic returned from the meeting, he informed us about that, and so at that Staff meeting they tried to make some decisions and reach some conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll come back to that meeting later. But since we don't have a date yet, it might be not fully clear for the Chamber, but I'll come back to that later on. Do you know if Brano Grujic had relations with Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really can't say. I do know, as a member of the service, that Mr. Seselj was supposed to visit Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, the town of Bratunac, and his arrival was postponed, the reason being that at that time on this side, there were strong police forces and they were ready to arrest him. However, the Public Security Service at the time reported this, and Mr. Seselj gave up on the idea of visiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There might be a mistake in the transcript, Mr. Dutertre. At line 10 of page 28, the page we have here, in the English version it is said "Mali Zvornik," in the English version, whereas it seems that in the French version you said "the municipality of Zvornik or Prevnik [phoen]."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In English, page 28, line 10, the witness said: "When the meeting was organised in Mali Zvornik --" It's not up to me to give evidence. I don't see any mistake to be corrected here, but we'll come back to that at a later stage, because we'll take it in chronological order. I wanted him to give information about relations with the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, the Prosecution asked you at some point if you were aware of relations between Grujic and Mr. Seselj, inducing us to believe that Mr. Seselj was internationally known. Who was Mr. Seselj for you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj was the president of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you knew that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Since the Prosecutor's already forgotten about it, we should set the time period, because the witness said that I was supposed to visit Bratunac. When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: That was exactly the point of my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the Prosecution will make everything clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, it's exactly the point of my next question, but you're leading me to it. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes. It was still unclear in the chronology, but what time period was that visit by Mr. Seselj to Bratunac planned?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I can't be precise as to the date, but I do know with certainty that the visit by Mr. Seselj was announced and that, from Tuzla, the Public Security Centre there sent a special unit, and they were present in the police station throughout the time and waited for his visit to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Maybe so we can clarify matters, were you already in your position in Zvornik or weren't you in your position? Is it before or after October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, after October. I think it was in 1992, in the first few months of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Understood. So to wrap up on the political forces and the political composition of the municipality, do you know the ethnic makeup of Zvornik today?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Today, there are very few Muslims there; exclusively a Serb population. I don't think there are even 10 per cent of Muslims there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Good. Now, let's move on to military forces. Do you know if JNA forces were stationed in the Zvornik area between October 1991 and April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. In a place called Celopek, there was a complete armoured battalion that was withdrawn from Jastrebarsko, from Croatia, so it was stationed there in Celopek.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What time did the battalion arrive in Celopek, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: That was during their withdrawal from Croatia, that period, and they were located in this place called Celopek. And after that, at the bridge in Karakaj, they set up the tanks, they positioned the tanks there, and also at Divic, on the hydroelectric power plant there; dam, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Let's try and be more accurate. Could you indicate a month during which they arrived? Was it in November, December? Could you give us more detail to shed like on the subject?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: The end of 1991. I think it was November or December 1991, when they returned. Perhaps earlier, but certainly then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who was the commander of this JNA military unit?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: You mean the unit that was in Celopek, their commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I don't know the man's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who is Colonel Tacic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: He was an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, and he had his seat in the barracks in Tuzla. That's where his headquarters were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Understood. Were there members of the TO in Zvornik over that period between October 1991 and April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Apart from the Territorial Defence and the JNA, did you notice whether any volunteers arrived between October 1991 and April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but could you explain what you mean, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know if paramilitary volunteers arrived in the area of Zvornik between October 1991 and April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution, in the question there are "paramilitary volunteers." The question is somewhat complicated. The Prosecution asked you about volunteers, saying "paramilitary volunteers." Were there paramilitary units? You know what are paramilitary units, do you, and what is a volunteer for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do know that. The volunteers were the people who were outside the system, outside the system. The system was the regular army and the regular police force, and also regular was the Territorial Defence. Everybody else was outside that system, and that's where the volunteers belonged to, outside, those who nobody could engage according to the law and pursuant to the law, but they came in of their own will, voluntarily, or they were persuaded to report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, you're a police inspector. You're well educated and well informed. According to the law at the time on defence matters, weren't volunteers taken into account, people who would volunteer to be joining regular units? Wasn't that a possibility legally provided for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During that period of time, the system that we had was as follows: In case of imminent danger of war, the Secretariat for National Defence had a reserve force, and he would call that reserve force up in writing. The Ministry of the Interior had its reserve force, and they would be called up in writing. These were institutions regulated by law. Then there was the regular Yugoslav People's Army, so that way everybody knew where the reserve force was and had his reserve post. Everything that happened within that system was according to the system and governed by law. Everything else was irregular and outside the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, when you're saying that it was irregular and outside the law, are you saying that on the basis of Bosnian law or do you take into account the law still prevailing in former Yugoslavia? Because if I understood what you said correctly, here you're talking about volunteers or paramilitary people who are in the fighting fields, but the non-Bosnian fighting fields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, the laws that were in force were Yugoslav laws. They were in force for everyone, and that included us in Bosnia. So we all acted pursuant to the laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying "at that time." What year was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm thinking of all the time up until -- at least as far as Zvornik is concerned, April of 1992, and I'm speaking for Zvornik. After that period, for a time the laws were still applied, but then new laws were in force because the states became independent, they proclaimed their own constitutions. New constitutions and new laws were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your country, Bosnia-Herzegovina, became independent at which date, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm ashamed to say it, but I really don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. But when the volunteers arrived, was it still Yugoslavia, or Bosnia-Herzegovina already existed with a president, Izetbegovic, so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Before the arrival of the volunteers in Zvornik, Bosnia-Herzegovina was a sovereign and independent state, independently recognised, before the arrival, before their arrival. So all volunteers that came in arrived to a state that was internationally recognised and independent, sovereign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you certain of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, you can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you said you knew something about those volunteers. Can you tell us what you knew about them?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: As a member of the service at that time in Zvornik, I worked as assistant commander of the police station, and all the work that that entailed. After April 1992, four volunteers who had arrived from Serbia were arrested at one of the barricades that was erected by the citizens of Zvornik. They were stopped there, taken into custody, and handed over to us at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I will come back to that incident at a later stage. To stick to the chronological order once again, and it might clarify a question I've just asked. What day did the attack on Zvornik take place?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: The attack on Zvornik took place on the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Understood. Okay, I will now try to go over the period between October 1991 and April 1992, in a chronological manner, so as to point to some salient events. The first question: What were the relations like between Serbs and Bosnian when you arrived in Zvornik in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Relations were good, proper. At least my service, working in the field, we had contacts with lots of people, and the relationships weren't bad. They were good.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You explained that official positions were allocated on the basis of electoral results. When you arrived in October 1991, what were the SDS claims on position allocation and administration? Did the SDS accepting of the allocation? Did they object to the allocation or was their position neutral on that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Well, what I can say is this: When I arrived in Zvornik and was sent to the Public Security Station, I came across the situation as it was. However, the Serbian Democratic Party at the time was not satisfied with its positions in the distribution of power and authority, and it demanded that it be changed to its advantage. There were negotiations that went on for days. The leaders of the SDA and SDS held consultations about the different posts and adjustments that were supposed to be made, and when the Serbian Democratic Party didn't like something, they decided to reach those posts by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know whether crisis staffs were set up within the local branches of SDS and SDA at Zvornik, and at what period of time?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I know for a fact that the crisis staffs existed at the time both in the Serbian Democratic Party and in the Party of Democratic Action. I know that for a fact, that is, that they existed. When they were founded, I don't know. I cannot confirm that. I do know that they convened and met, and the Crisis Staff of the Party of Democratic Action met on two occasions at the police station, where I, as a present officer, wanted to hear what was going on and was present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. When you say you don't know exactly when these were set up, could you tell us this: At the time you arrived in Zvornik in 1991, whether these crisis staffs in the SDA and SDS existed already or not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I believe that they did. The task of the crisis staffs at the time was as follows, and this is what our police sources tell us and the other information that we had at the time: The crisis staffs had the task of homogenizing each one, its own ethnic structure, and to arm them and prepare them for war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. You anticipated my next question. Did you notice - this is something you mentioned - that they were wearing weapons or were arming each --

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Getting weapons?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Armed. The Serbs were being armed by the army, and we know that for a fact because military lorries actually brought in weapons and distributed it to the Serbs. The Bosniaks, on the other hand, bought weapons and they also armed themselves, but the Serbs had a much better supply and much more pieces of weapons, because they received them, and the Bosniaks bought their armaments. That is the difference. But both peoples were arming.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: According to you, according to what you know, when did the Serbian and Bosniak people start?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Zvornik, the situation was like that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Did you notice any incidents while you were in Zvornik, between October 1991 and April 1992, incidents which could have been ethnic in nature?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Incidents of an ethnic nature started happening, and we, as the police, were confronted with huge problems, trying to prevent such incidents from happening, and to simply calm tensions and to see to the establishment of some normal order in order to prevent any further escalations of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How many incidents do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: There were many minor incidents, but there are two incidents which merit attention, and I'm going to elaborate on these two on this occasion. When I arrived in Zvornik, one of these incidents had already happened in a place which is also in Zvornik Municipality, in a place called Kiseljak. A taxi driver was killed there brutally. His throat was slit. And this was a citizen -- a Serbian -- a Serb citizen of Zvornik. This incident created enormous problems for us, and we sought to shed light on it in every possible way. But we never managed to do so, because we were prevented because the war. I believe that this was orchestrated incident at the time in order to, indeed, create an incident situation between the Bosniaks and the Serbs, to raise tensions and to give -- and to provoke the erection of barricades and all the other things that attended the situation. The second incident was in Sapna. There was a column of soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army approaching. Whenever they passed through these places, they would also have reservists with them, and they would shoot from the columns at the settlements that they were passing through, at the mosques and different buildings, and the locals returned fire. The locals of the village of Sapna returned fire, and one military officer, who I believe was a warrant officer, was killed. And that is the second incident which happened and which was also used as calls for -- also brought about a tumultuous situation and the heightening of tensions. Although we had the Tuzla police from their centre actually undertaking the investigation, and the investigation was conducted by an investigative judge, with Mr. Marinko Vasilic also from our station as representing the Serbs, and Mr. Fadil Mujic representing the Muslims, we composed a team intentionally in such a way for them to see to the observance of the regularity of procedure, because we didn't want anyone to tell us that we didn't act according to proper procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. It might be time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, please, now, because we'll only have one break today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: The simplest question to begin with: The second incident, what date did that occur on, please?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say with precision, but I do know that at the time I was one of the commanding officers in the police station in Zvornik. So it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned that the first incident had been orchestrated. Could you explain this to us? Who had orchestrated this first incident, according to you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I couldn't confirm that, but according to our information, the information available to the police and the sources available to the police from our intelligence sources on the ground, actually told us that this was done -- had been done deliberately, that it was done in order to heighten inter-ethnic tensions and to have the situation in the area deteriorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. If this is the right time to have a break, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall have the break now and resume at a quarter past 4.00, and then we will run on until 6.00 without having a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please let me know how much time I have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You still have a lot of time left. Madam Registrar, could you give us the countdown, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution used 47 minutes so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, what happened in Celopek with members of the Serb police in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: At the time, a review was conducted of what they called the Serb militia, the Serb police. These were policemen who also were part of the Public Security Station in Zvornik, and they were on the active force. This lineup and review of that unit was carried out by Spasojevic, the then commander of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Were there only Serbian policemen or also Bosnian police officers, and if not, why?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: There were no Bosniak policemen among them. It was only Serb policemen who attended the -- this event, which was some sort of a dress rehearsal of the Serbian police force in the town of Zvornik. This was the last preparation, as it were, that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How did you find out about the event? What was your source of information?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: My source of information was the intelligence available to the police, which was present there, and they wrote official records, official notes, which were submitted to us, and we discussed them on the next day at the meeting of the Staff Collegium in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was discussed at that meeting, what were the conclusions of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: The staff meeting at the police station met very often and convened on a daily basis, if necessary, and on the agenda were different problems about the situation -- concerning the situation on the ground, et cetera. On that occasion, I asked Mr. Dragan Spasojevic, in connection with this problem, I said, "Dragan, please tell us, what kind of a review was this that you undertook, what does it signify? Who was obliged to attend?" Dragan just laughed, and he told me, "Well, this is the police of the future Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you clarify at what point in time the incident in Celopek took place; what month, what year?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I believe it was the end of February or the beginning of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a few dates. Just so you know where you are, these are dates in the Prosecution's document on the 27th [Realtime transcript read in error "28th"] of March, 1992, Republika Srpska was officially proclaimed in Pale. On the 27th of March, not the 28th. And on the 6th of April, 1992, the United States of America and the European Community officially recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state. So these are two dates which might be helpful to you and us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Presiding Judge. This is extremely precious information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What happened in April, April 1st, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... the United States of America and the European Community recognised independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina means absolutely nothing. I insist that you give the witness the date of the admission of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the United Nations. That can be, in a certain sense, legally relevant. The fact that the Americans and the European Community actually recognised it is something that you can really discard as totally immaterial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, to be part of the United States, you need to be an independent state, so not even that date would be helpful to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We also recall the issue of the United Nations, but that comes at a later stage. Before you become a member of the United States -- the United Nations, sorry, you first need to become a state, and for that you need to be recognised. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I repeat my question --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an additional objection. Why did it not occur to you to say on which date Russia recognised it, and China and India, on what day did China recognise? Why do you always give precedence to America and the European Community, which to me are hostile states?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have the dates, you can provide them to us. I've read the Prosecution document which is attached to the document. It's attachment 1. So I referred to the aforesaid document. Now, if you have any other known date, the dates at which Russia and China and India recognised, we will acknowledge those dates quite willingly. But so far, I don't have these dates in the Prosecution documents. Okay, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not going to interfere in the examination-in-chief, and I'm not going to provide you with this information. I'm just stating my objection. The one who gave you the previous information should supply you with the rest of the information. This is the examination-in-chief, and I'm not going to interfere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Bosnia was admitted in the United Nations in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened on the 1st of April, 1992, in Sarajevo, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of April in Sarajevo, we had a scheduled meeting of all members of the police. We all had to be present up there, and by our presence, to show our shared commitment to having a united police force remain as such in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So we were against any divisions on an ethnic basis or any other sorts of divisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What ethnic members of the police were present at that meeting on the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: No one was present of the Serb policemen at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice whether Serbs or people of their family left Zvornik at the beginning of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did so on a number of occasions, and I believe personally observed that. This took place during the weekends. They would leave in the afternoons. They would pack and put whatever they could into their cars, and they would then cross the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And exactly how long before the attack on Zvornik did they start leaving the town?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Almost a month or a bit more than that before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Now I'll come back to the second incident mentioned by two witnesses. You will remember that the witnesses mentioned two incidents, one with a Serb taxi driver and others with shots in Sapna, so I'd like to jog your memory, Mr. Witness, regarding the date of the incident. Mr. Alic, do you remember testifying or providing evidence on the 13th of July, 1993, before an investigator of the Tribunal? It's a written statement.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I will read part of paragraph 4, page 2, of that statement, and I'll start reading: [In English] "Ever since the war in the former Yugoslavia started, JNA troops went through the Zvornik area and on their way to the battlefields in Croatia on a regular basis."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. There's absolutely no reason for the Prosecutor to read out this portion of the statement. He didn't ask any questions referring to that at all, so now he has to remind the witness of a detail, so he has to ask the witness questions. And if the witness can't remember a detail, then he can go and say, "Well, this is what you said. Do you stand by that?" So it's, in fact, refreshing his memory on the basis of the statement. So that's very leading. There were leading questions before this as well, but I didn't decide to react because I didn't think it was too important. But this has gone too far now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, Mr. Seselj is voicing an objection I need to deal with. You're jogging the witness's memory by reading a paragraph from a statement. This statement was drafted over ten years ago, about twelve years ago, and understandably it's possible to forget about things that you've written and find twelve years before. I would be unable to remember that sort of thing. That is why you've read to him this paragraph, because you felt that there were uncertainties in his previous answers; is that the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness mentioned two incidents. He mentioned the date of the first one, approximately. He didn't indicate the date for the second incident. Regarding the second incident and the statement, a date is mentioned on the fourth line of the paragraph which I started quoting. This is why I wanted to ask the witness if that's what he remembers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go on, then. Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber has decided that the Prosecution can read the paragraph. Objection overruled. You don't have to comment on this issue. We understood that on the second incident, he was not able to give accurate dates. This is why we are reading the paragraph to him, to jog his memory. What do you, yourself, do? When you have your own statements, you read them to a witness. What is valid for you should be also valid for the Prosecution. Now, regarding whether it is a leading question or not, and the dangers in that, this is only a question to have a more accurate date. I don't see where the danger of a leading question would be. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I want to say is this: You cannot say that what holds true for me holds true for the Prosecutor. There are a set of rules for the examination-in-chief and other rules for the cross-examination. The Prosecutor could have asked the witness whether he remembers having said this in the statement, that the event in Sapna happened on the 5th of April, 1992, on such-and-such a page, and not reading an entire paragraph from the statement. That is not refreshing his memory, in the sense of the Appeals Chamber ruling. What he can do is say, "You said here that it was the 5th of April. What do you have to say to that?" Because it's in my interest to hear when the exact date was, and it was in fact three days before the final clash in Zvornik took place. So it's in my interests for that to be stated. But in principle, the way in which the witness's memory is refreshed and by reading out this whole passage is not the right way to go about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As Mr. Seselj was speaking, I was looking at the paragraph. The date is on the fourth line of that paragraph, so read up until the fourth line, until the comma, the full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have said the date myself. Maybe I would have been blamed for not reading the paragraph. If I read the paragraph, I'm now being blamed for not giving the date. But Mr. Seselj has given the date, the 5th of April, 1992. Now I can ask the question directly to the witness. Thank you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Alic, that the second incident you mentioned before took place on the 5th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that I cannot confirm the exact date. But now I've heard what the date was, so I do believe that that is correct, that it was, indeed, that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alic. You indicated that Mr. Mujic and Mr. Vasilic took part in the investigation. Could you tell us what happened to them on the 5th of April, 1992, during their investigation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: This investigation was conducted by the investigating judge from Tuzla. It was under his leadership, and the crime police from Tuzla, the Security Centre, carried out an on-site examination, and we were included in the team, and Fadil Mujic, the chief of the crime police, and Vasilic, Marinko, supervised it, the assistant commander of the police station, they supervised it. But the investigation was never completed, because three days later in the town of Zvornik, everything had already escalated and everyone went their own way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did anything happen to Mr. Vasilic and Mr. Mujic on that day, on the 5th of April, 1992, in the course of their investigation, which we now know didn't --

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, at one of the barracks that was located between Karakaj and Sapna.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who controlled the road blockage?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: The locals, the citizens, the Serbs who were from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And what happened to Mr. Mujic and Vasilic at the roadblock controlled by the Serbian inhabitants in the village?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: They -- to all intents and purposes, they were arrested there, and Mr. Mujic and him could not identify the people who had arrested them, but they underwent great unpleasantness, and then even told that the town of Zvornik could be attacked and razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How did you find out about this? Did they tell you about it or other people did?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Well, that story was told at the professional staff meeting, and I was present there, and it was held the very next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who told that story?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic and Mr. Vasilic. Both of them were members of the Collegium, the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In the night between 5th and 6th of April, 1992, what happened in Zvornik and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: In Zvornik, what happened was this: When the policemen, Serb policemen, left the legal, regular Public Security Station, taking with them a certain quantity of weapons and equipment, they went to Karakaj, to the Standard building, where they set up a new police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And during that night, did something happen regarding access to the city of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. On all the approach roads, barricades were set up, which quite literally cut off the town of Zvornik from all the other places and prevented exit and entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who set up the roadblocks in the night between the 5th and 6th of April, 1992, on the road to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: They were set up by the citizens of Zvornik of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you remember drawing a map during your written statement to the OTP investigator in 1997, showing the location of these roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I did give statements, and I did make some sketches, but I can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I want to see this 1997 statement. All I have is the 1996 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1997 statement was communicated -- disclosed to the accused, so he should have it. But we might be able to print it out again, but he received it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I did receive it at some point, but I have no trace of it. I just have the 1996 statement in front of me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was communicated to the accused. I'm formal on that. But we'll try to print it as soon as possible. I'd like to display Exhibit 65 ter 7223, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, is this drawing the one you did yourself at the time in 1997? That's the English version appearing. Do you recognise your signature at the bottom of the drawing?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: The various stations set up after the reserve policemen were mobilised, you talked about Pilica, Orahovac. Do these various stations appear on the drawing?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you show us, on the sketch, what the double lines in read show? They appear on what seems to represent a road.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Those red lines, double lines, denote the place where barricades had been erected.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to tender the sketch into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P439.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, what was the Bosnian inhabitants' in Zvornik reaction when the aforesaid barricades were set up?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Well, you can well imagine what the reaction was when the barricades suddenly crop up and stop all traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You indicated that during the night, the Serbian policemen left. Could you tell us the names of some of these Serbian policemen who left Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, the then commander Dragan Spasojevic was the commander up there, and his assistants were Slavko Tadic and Marinko Vasilic, and they were assistants in this other Zvornik Public Security Station, and all the other Serb policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to move on now to the 7th of April, 1992, in Zvornik. What happened in the morning of the 7th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: The 7th of April, 1992, that was a -- well, just prior to the war, a state of siege, and a crisis staff meeting was held. I was present to see what was being done there, and also present were Abdulah Pasic, the mayor, Alija Kapidzic, and various other people, and they said at that staff meeting that they had to go to Mali Zvornik because they were called there, because Arkan was waiting for them there, and that they were to conduct certain negotiations over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You mentioned that Arkan was waiting for them there, Abdulah Pasic and Alija Kapidzic. How had they been informed, through what means?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: They were called -- well, the liaison was Mr. Brano Grujic. Mr. Brano Grujic attended the meeting, himself, in Mali Zvornik, at the meeting in the Jezero Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you -- well, what happened at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: At the meeting, they failed to reach any agreement. And after returning back from the meeting, they informed us what had happened over there, and Mr. Pasic and Mr. Kapidzic said that they had many unpleasant situations there and that Arkan sort of slapped them, and that they had to compile a written report to the effect that there were 7.000 Green Berets in the town of Zvornik and that this was some kind of a Muslim army that was a threat to the Serbs and instilled fear in them. However, that was not true, not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. On the 7th of April, 1992, did you see Colonel Tacic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Colonel Tacic said that he was going to come to the municipal building from Tuzla, and the chief gave me orders that I should go there and escort Colonel Tacic from the first barricade, from the Karakaj direction. I forget the name of the place, Tereze [phoen] or something. Anyway, I escorted him to the municipal building, and then I waited for the meeting to be over to escort him back to Tuzla. Now, in -- well, I talked to Colonel Tacic while escorting him, and he asked me what was going on. And I said, "Well, Colonel, I ought to ask you what was going on, because I see that all the military equipment is here, all the military weapons, so I assume you should know what's going on." But he never answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Just a point of detail. You told us that you took him to the mayor. We mentioned Mali Zvornik a few moments ago. Do you mean the mayor of Mali Zvornik or Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Zvornik Municipality, headquarters in Zvornik, not Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. What time was it, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: It was about, well, between 12.00 and 2.00 p.m. That's when he arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A point of detail that could be important. You escorted Colonel Tacic, and after that you take him back because he has to attend a meeting at the town hall or municipality. When he tells you, "What is happening here," was it on the outbound journey or when you went back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we were arriving, because he, himself, could not pass through that barricade, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So when he is saying, "What is happening," did you have the feeling that he had no idea of what was going on, or did he say that by the by and you felt that he was fully informed? What was your feeling about this at that time? I mean, one doesn't escort a colonel every day, so this is something which you certainly remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he was having me on that day. I think that he was in complete control of the situation, that he had all the information, firsthand information, about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's assume that he wanted to mislead or abuse you. Why do you think he wanted to do that? Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps he was afraid, he was afraid. He certainly knew -- he knew the date of the attack, and the organisation, and now he was coming to the center of town which was only populated by the Muslims and police members at that point in time. So he was coming into a centre where the Muslims were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If what you say is true, if you were moving into an area which was controlled by the Muslims, he might have been risking his life. So what was the point of going there? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't present at that meeting held in the municipal building. It was the party presidents and Abdulah Pasic and Brano Grujic who were there and the rest, from the leadership of both sides, both political parties. Colonel Tacic had already positioned his tanks at the bridge at Karakaj a long time ago, and at the dam, Divic, so that he had all the information at his disposal, and nothing could have happened without his knowing about it. And before that, I set up patrols of our police force at the time and members of the army so that together we could perform our duties and provide security for vital facilities. So the army was included in all that to a maximum degree and disposed of all the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly? You were there to ensure his safety while he was in the Zvornik area, where only the Muslims were left, the Bosnian were left?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and I escorted him from the barricade to the municipal building. Then I waited in front of the municipal building after the meeting to take him back in the direction he wanted to go. Of course, before the barricade. I wasn't able to go through the barricade itself, because I would have run the risk of danger, whereas it wasn't dangerous for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know who attended the meeting on the Bosnian side at the town hall in the presence of Colonel Tacic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Abdulah Pasic, the mayor; Alija Kapidzic was there. He was in the Secretariat for National Defence. Brano Grujic was the president of the Serbian Democratic Party, and Jovo Mijatovic, yes, Mijatovic, he was the president of the executive powers of the Zvornik Municipality, the Executive Council, and some other people on both sides whose names I don't know, and there was my chief of my police station, Osman Mustafic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's working again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I don't know if this was a translation issue. Did you say "Mijatovic" or "Jovo Ivanovic?"

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Ivanovic, Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Did you discover what the outcome of this meeting was? Did you discover what had been decided there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: The result of the meeting was nil. The meeting was expected to reach an agreement, and to provide protection -- for the JNA to provide protection, but since at that time there was strong pressure and propaganda for the Serbian Democratic Party to be handed over power, and that weapons be laid down and the town handed over, those were conditions that were completely unacceptable at the time, and that's how the whole thing ended, without any major decisions and results.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What happened in the afternoon between Arkan and the negotiators Pasic and Kapidzic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: At that meeting - that's what they called it - they told us, both Pasic and Kapidzic, that Arkan on the occasion had slapped them around a few times and placed a knife under their throats and provided a piece of paper so they could write down certain statements, which they in fact did do. And upon their return to the police station, they informed us about this and said, "We did what we did under pressure." Now, if you consider that they should be prosecuted, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you mentioned Arkan. Who was Arkan, in your eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Arkan was a man from amongst the ranks of the Serb people who had proclaimed himself some kind of military leader over there. He had a group of volunteers, and he went to various battle fronts with them. And those who belonged to him were known as Arkan's Tigers, his men were known as Arkan's Tigers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you clarify one point for us, please. Between Arkan and the two negotiators, there was one meeting in the morning, one meeting in the afternoon, is that right, or was there just one meeting? Could you specify, please? We're still talking about the 7th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: I believe that there was just one meeting held, and that was the first and the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. How did the town mayor react to this meeting between Arkan and the two negotiators; did he take any decision?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: Upon returning from that meeting, the Crisis Staff met hastily in order to inform us what transpired at the meeting. In view of the fact that no conclusion or a decision could be taken that could actually redress the situation and bring some sort of a solution, but only featured pressures and ultimatums, it was these ultimatums that were discussed at the Crisis Staff meeting. One of the ultimatums was that by 10.00 on the next day, all arms were to be laid down, that meaning the police had legal weapons and that which had been collected by the Territorial Defence, and that authority was to be handed over or that there would be war. Simply, the town had to be abandoned. That was the option that we were confronted with, or war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What option did the Crisis Staff take?

utterances.speaker: ASIM ALIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff decided not to give in to the ultimatum, that they would not lay down their arms, that we would defend the citizens, the people and their property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there was an ultimatum on the 7th of April to disarm. This we understand. If I reminded you of a date a few moments ago, this date was that of the 6th of April, when Bosnia-Herzegovina had been recognised at that time, was this all factored in by the Crisis Staff or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had in mind -- I have in mind that Bosnia-Herzegovina had been recognised. Everybody knew this, but one of the sides did not recognise that fact, nor does so today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
